meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Abandon all hope, ye who enter here'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Dante's line (Inferno III.9) — but 'Abandon all hope, ye who enter here' is a popularized rearrangement; Cary's 1814 original read 'All hope abandon.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 1265 – 1321 · Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line by Dante — the inscription over the Gate of Hell in the Inferno, Canto III, line 9 (“Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch’intrate”), written c. 1308–1320. The exact English wording, though, is a translation, and no single canonical version reads precisely this way: H. F. Cary’s 1814 rendering gave “All hope abandon ye who enter here.”

source.excerpt: “Before me things create were none, save things / Eternal, and eternal I endure. / All hope abandon ye who enter here.”
trail: The line is Inferno, Canto III, line 9 — the last words of the inscription over the Gate of Hell — in Dante’s Divine Comedy, written c. 1308–1320. The original Italian is “Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch’intrate” ↗.

The exact English wording is a translation — and matches no single canonical one. H. F. Cary’s 1814 version reads “All hope abandon ye who enter here” ↗; Longfellow (1867) gave “All hope abandon, ye who enter in!” and Norton (1891) “Leave every hope, ye who enter!”
The smoothed popular form “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here” is a later rearrangement ↗ that became the standard English idiom, not the wording Cary or any single translator actually printed.
source.excerptNote: The closing lines of the Gate of Hell inscription in H. F. Cary’s 1814 translation. The original Italian ninth line is “Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch’intrate”; the familiar “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here” is a later, smoother rearrangement of renderings like this one.

source.rightsNote: Dante’s Italian original (c. 1320) has been in the public domain for centuries, and the 19th-century English translations this wording descends from — H. F. Cary (1814), Longfellow (1867), Norton (1891) — are all long out of copyright. The exact popular phrasing “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here” is an anonymous rearrangement rather than a modern copyrighted translation, so no live rights attach to it.

author.metaLine: c. 1265–1321 · Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy
author.bio: Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet whose three-part Divine Comedy (Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso), written in the Tuscan vernacular between roughly 1308 and 1320, became the foundational masterwork of Italian literature. Its first canticle, the Inferno, follows the pilgrim and his guide Virgil through the Gate of Hell, whose inscription closes with this line. Dante is traditionally called il Sommo Poeta, “the Supreme Poet.”

misattribution.heading: The catch: right author, re-worded quote
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Dante is correct — this really is his line. What almost everyone gets wrong is the wording: the phrasing people quote matches no actual published translation.

items.who: “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here”
items.why: The famous phrasing is a later rearrangement of the English translations. H. F. Cary’s 1814 version reads “All hope abandon ye who enter here” ↗; Longfellow (1867) gave “All hope abandon, ye who enter in!” and Norton (1891) “Leave every hope, ye who enter!” — none reads exactly the popular form.

items.who: “Abandon hope, all ye who enter here”
items.why: In this common variant the word “all” is shifted so it seems to modify “ye” (everyone who enters) rather than “hope.” Dante’s “ogne speranza” means “all hope” — it is the hope that is total, not the crowd.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the line are genuinely Dante’s — Inferno III.9 — but “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here” is a popularized English rendering, not the wording of any single canonical translation.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: In the Inferno, Dante the pilgrim and his guide Virgil reach the Gate of Hell, which bears a nine-line inscription spoken as if the gate itself were the narrator. The line is its chilling final word — the threshold of no return before the descent through the nine circles.

Because it is a translated line, English has never settled on one wording. The version that won out in popular use, “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here,” is smoother than any of the scholarly renderings — which is exactly why it, rather than Cary’s or Longfellow’s, became the phrase carved onto everything from doorways to memes.
